title: Asato ma: the breath the demons couldn't pierce
hookLine: the gods audition every sense to sing their victory chant, and only the plain breath can't be corrupted
tomorrow: "I am" — the self alone, afraid, then desiring

lines: LEAD ME FROM THE UNREAL TO THE REAL.
cards: Lead me from the unreal to the real. From darkness to light. From death to the deathless.
It's chanted in Sanskrit before classes, pujas, yoga sessions, school assemblies. And it comes from today's chapter of the Brihadaranyaka, at the end of a strange little war story.
The gods and the demons, both children of the creator Prajapati, are fighting over the worlds. The gods' plan: win with a chant. All they need is a singer the demons can't corrupt.
So they start auditioning the parts of the body.

teach.h: SPEECH SINGS, AND KEEPS SOME FOR ITSELF.
teach.b: First they ask speech. Speech sings for them, but keeps the best part for itself: the pleasure of speaking well. The demons rush at it and pierce it with evil.
That, says the text, is why we say things we shouldn't. Then smell. Then the eye.
Then the ear. Then the mind.

teach.h: EYE, EAR, MIND: EACH ONE PIERCED.
teach.b: Each one sings, keeps something back, and gets pierced. That's why we see, hear and think things we wish we hadn't.

teach.h: THE DEMONS SHATTER ON THE BREATH.
teach.b: Last, the gods turn to the breath in the mouth, the plain breath that keeps you alive. Breath sings. The demons rush at it too, and they shatter, the text says, like a clod of earth thrown against a stone.
Why breath? One common reading: it took nothing for itself. It sang for everyone.
A few weeks ago, the Chandogya told this same battle in a few lines, and its longer story had breath win by threatening to leave.
Here the battle is told in full, and on this reading breath wins because it's the one faculty that doesn't grab. Then breath carries each of the others past death. Speech becomes fire.
The eye becomes the sun. The ear becomes the directions. The mind becomes the moon.
And the chapter ends with the chant: asato ma sad gamaya, tamaso ma jyotir gamaya, mrityor ma amritam gamaya. The text explains its own words. The unreal is death; the real is the deathless.
Darkness is death; light is the deathless.
In its home, this chant is a prayer to be carried the way breath carries the senses.

how: Many Hindus chant asato ma sad gamaya at the start of study, worship or a gathering, and teachers often explain its three lines as the movement from death to the deathless.

o: the victory chant the gods sang to win
breath, the life-force in every body
the mind that steers all the senses

games.q: who became what — tap the pairs.
p: pierced by evil, then became fire

s: the chant "lead me from the unreal to the real" comes from the Brihadaranyaka
in the story, speech wins the war for the gods
speech kept something for itself and was pierced. the plain breath won.
the text explains its own chant
the unreal and darkness are death; the real and light are the deathless.

games.q: you're one of the gods. speech, smell, the eye, the ear and the mind have all sung, and the demons pierced every one. who do you ask next?
o: the mind again, louder this time.
the plain breath in the mouth.
give up and let the demons have the worlds.
games.why: they ask the breath. it keeps nothing for itself, and the demons break on it like a clod of earth thrown against a stone.

practice: Let the breath move without steering it, and notice how it takes nothing for itself: it comes in, feeds every part of you, and goes. When a thought, a sound or a worry grabs you, let it be, and come back to the breath under it.
If you pray, you can say the old chant silently on the out-breath: from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to the deathless.

wordCard.voice: Prana, breath, the life-force. In this story prana is the one faculty the demons couldn't pierce, because it sang for everyone and kept nothing back.

orig.note: Sanskrit prāṇa: breath, the life-force. pra (forth) + an (to breathe).

carryVoice: Your line: breath is untouched by evil. Tomorrow, the first words ever spoken. Until then.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.3.1–27 (the gods, the demons and the breath)
